newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua president aims to resolve property issue.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua president aims to resolve property issue.

text.p: Nicaragua's impoverished economy cannot be helped until the status of some 200,000 properties confiscated during the leftist Sandinista regime is resolved, President Arnoldo Aleman said on Monday.

"If this acute property problem is not resolved then I think any economic programme for this country will fail," Aleman, whose right-wing Liberal Alliance government took power on Jan. 10, said on the talk show Buenos Dias.

He made a top priority of resolving the bitter ownership disputes surrounding the properties confiscated during the 1979-1990 Sandinista government. Liberal and Sandinista delegations began negotiations to resolve the property problem on Jan. 27 but the talks broke off amid mutual accusations of intransigency at the end of February.

Aleman said his government planned to give legal land titles to the thousands of poor families who received confiscated land and compensate the former owners. But the government will make wealthy Sandinistas and the party itself return or pay for the confiscated properties in their hands.

Uncertainty over land ownership and the threat of violence between the occupants of confiscated land and the former owners have long scared away investors from Nicaragua. Aleman on Monday accused the Sandinistas of trying to undermine his government's free-market economic programme and called on them to return to the bargaining table for Nicaragua's sake.
"They know that if we succeed in dragging Nicaragua from its poverty, which almost passes from poverty into misery, the Sandinista party will never return to power," he said.

According to the Ministry of the Economy, Nicaragua in 1978 had an annual per capita income of about $1,200, but by 1996 this had fallen to $469, making it the second poorest country in the Americas. The government predicts the economy will grow by 6.8 percent in 1997.
